claim: Bacteriophage T7 infects Escherichia coli.
source: Bacteriophage T7 infects Escherichia coli and evades the host restriction/modification system.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Studier, 1972; Krüger and Schroeder, 1981; Hausmann and Messerschmid, 1988).

claim: The Ocr protein of T7 exists as a dimer mimicking DNA.
source: The Ocr protein of T7 was shown to exist as a dimer mimicking DNA and to bind to host restriction enzymes, thus preventing the degradation of the viral genome by the host.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2) and citations (Walkinshaw et al., 2002).

claim: Ocr binds to host restriction enzymes, preventing degradation of the viral genome.
source: The Ocr protein of T7 was shown to exist as a dimer mimicking DNA and to bind to host restriction enzymes, thus preventing the degradation of the viral genome by the host.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations (Studier, 1975; Walkinshaw et al., 2002).

claim: Ocr can inhibit host transcription by directly binding to bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP).
source: Here we report that Ocr can also inhibit host transcription by directly binding to bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) and competing with the recruitment of RNAP by sigma factors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including gel filtration, MST, and in vitro transcription assays (Figures 1, 5, 6).

claim: Ocr competes with the recruitment of RNAP by sigma factors.
source: Here we report that Ocr can also inhibit host transcription by directly binding to bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) and competing with the recruitment of RNAP by sigma factors.
evidence: This is supported by gel mobility shift assays and MST experiments showing Ocr can disrupt RNAP-sigma holoenzyme formation (Figure 6).

claim: The structures of Ocr bound to RNAP were determined using cryo electron microscopy.
source: Using cryo electron microscopy, we determined the structures of Ocr bound to RNAP.
evidence: This is supported by the cryoEM data and structural models presented (Figures 2, 3, 4).

claim: An Ocr dimer binds to RNAP in the cleft where key regions of sigma bind and where DNA resides during transcription synthesis.
source: The structures show that an Ocr dimer binds to RNAP in the cleft, where key regions of sigma bind and where DNA resides during transcription synthesis, thus providing a structural basis for the transcription inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing Ocr occupying the DNA binding channel (Figures 2, 3).

claim: T7 genome encodes 56 proteins.
source: The T7 genome encodes 56 proteins with many functioning as structural proteins for the bacteriophage.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge about T7.

claim: T7 proteins gp0.7, gp2 and gp5.7 inhibit cellular transcription.
source: For example, proteins gp0.7, gp2 and gp5.7 inhibit cellular transcription (Cámara et al., 2010; Tabib-Salazar et al., 2018) whereas gp0.3 inhibits restriction/modification (RM) enzymes (Studier, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gp0.3 inhibits restriction/modification (RM) enzymes.
source: For example, proteins gp0.7, gp2 and gp5.7 inhibit cellular transcription (Cámara et al., 2010; Tabib-Salazar et al., 2018) whereas gp0.3 inhibits restriction/modification (RM) enzymes (Studier, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Studier, 1975.

claim: Gp0.3 is the first T7 gene expressed after infection.
source: Gp0.3 is the first T7 gene expressed after infection and T7 variants lacking gene 0.3 were shown to have genomes susceptible to E. coli RM systems (Studier, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Studier, 1975.

claim: T7 variants lacking gene 0.3 have genomes susceptible to E. coli RM systems.
source: Gp0.3 is the first T7 gene expressed after infection and T7 variants lacking gene 0.3 were shown to have genomes susceptible to E. coli RM systems (Studier, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Studier, 1975.

claim: The 117 amino acid protein gp0.3 was named Overcome Classical Restriction (Ocr).
source: Subsequently the 117 amino acid protein gp0.3 was named Overcome Classical Restriction (Ocr) (Krüger and Schroeder, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krüger and Schroeder, 1981.

claim: Ocr forms a dimer that mimics the structure of a slightly bent 20 base pair B-form DNA.
source: Ocr is abundantly expressed and forms a dimer that mimics the structure of a slightly bent 20 base pair B-form DNA (Issinger and Hausmann, 1972; Walkinshaw et al., 2002) and blocks the DNA binding grooves of the type I RM enzyme, preventing the degradation and modification of the T7 genome by the host.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Issinger and Hausmann, 1972 and Walkinshaw et al., 2002.

claim: Ocr blocks the DNA binding grooves of the type I RM enzyme.
source: Ocr is abundantly expressed and forms a dimer that mimics the structure of a slightly bent 20 base pair B-form DNA (Issinger and Hausmann, 1972; Walkinshaw et al., 2002) and blocks the DNA binding grooves of the type I RM enzyme, preventing the degradation and modification of the T7 genome by the host.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge about Ocr function.

claim: Type I RM enzymes are present in very low numbers, estimated at ~60 molecules per cell.
source: Intriguingly, Type I RM enzymes are present in very low numbers (estimated at ~60 molecules per cell [Kelleher and Raleigh, 1994]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kelleher and Raleigh, 1994.

claim: Ocr is abundantly expressed, estimated to be several hundreds of molecules per cell at least.
source: Since Ocr is a DNA mimicry protein, it is possible that the abundantly expressed Ocr (estimated to be several hundreds of molecules per cell at least) (Hausmann and Messerschmid, 1988) also interferes with other DNA processing systems of the host.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hausmann and Messerschmid, 1988.

claim: Early evidence of an interaction between Ocr and the host RNA polymerase (RNAP) was obtained using pull-down affinity chromatography.
source: Indeed early evidence of an interaction between Ocr and the host RNA polymerase (RNAP) was obtained using pull-down affinity chromatography (Ratner, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ratner, 1974.

claim: The large majority of transcription regulation is executed at the recruitment and initiation stage.
source: The large majority of transcription regulation, however, is executed at the recruitment and initiation stage (Browning and Busby, 2004; Hahn and Young, 2011; Browning and Busby, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Browning and Busby, 2004; Hahn and Young, 2011; Browning and Busby, 2016.

claim: E. coli has seven sigma factors which can be grouped into two classes.
source: E. coli has seven sigma factors which can be grouped into two classes, the σ70 class represented by σ70, responsible for transcribing housekeeping genes, and the σ54 class, responsible for transcribing stress-induced genes including phage infection (Feklístov et al., 2014; Browning and Busby, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Feklístov et al., 2014 and Browning and Busby, 2016.

claim: The σ70 class is responsible for transcribing housekeeping genes.
source: E. coli has seven sigma factors which can be grouped into two classes, the σ70 class represented by σ70, responsible for transcribing housekeeping genes, and the σ54 class, responsible for transcribing stress-induced genes including phage infection (Feklístov et al., 2014; Browning and Busby, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge.

claim: The σ54 class is responsible for transcribing stress-induced genes including phage infection.
source: E. coli has seven sigma factors which can be grouped into two classes, the σ70 class represented by σ70, responsible for transcribing housekeeping genes, and the σ54 class, responsible for transcribing stress-induced genes including phage infection (Feklístov et al., 2014; Browning and Busby, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge.

claim: The two large RNAP subunits β and β' form a crab claw structure that encloses the DNA binding cleft.
source: Specifically, the two large RNAP subunits β and β' form a crab claw structure that encloses the DNA binding cleft, accommodating the transcription bubble and the downstream double-stranded (ds) DNA (Bae et al., 2015; Zuo and Steitz, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bae et al., 2015 and Zuo and Steitz, 2015.

claim: Gp0.7 is a protein kinase that phosphorylates the E. coli RNAP-σ70, resulting in transcription termination at sites located between the early and middle genes on the T7 genome.
source: Gp0.7 is a protein kinase that phosphorylates the E. coli RNAP-σ70, resulting in transcription termination at sites located between the early and middle genes on the T7 genome, gp2 specifically inhibits σ70-dependent transcription initiation and gp5.7 inhibits σS, responsible for stationary phase adaptation (Bae et al., 2013; Tabib-Salazar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bae et al., 2013 and Tabib-Salazar et al., 2018.

claim: Gp2 specifically inhibits σ70-dependent transcription initiation.
source: Gp0.7 is a protein kinase that phosphorylates the E. coli RNAP-σ70, resulting in transcription termination at sites located between the early and middle genes on the T7 genome, gp2 specifically inhibits σ70-dependent transcription initiation and gp5.7 inhibits σS, responsible for stationary phase adaptation (Bae et al., 2013; Tabib-Salazar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bae et al., 2013 and Tabib-Salazar et al., 2018.

claim: Gp5.7 inhibits σS, responsible for stationary phase adaptation.
source: Gp0.7 is a protein kinase that phosphorylates the E. coli RNAP-σ70, resulting in transcription termination at sites located between the early and middle genes on the T7 genome, gp2 specifically inhibits σ70-dependent transcription initiation and gp5.7 inhibits σS, responsible for stationary phase adaptation (Bae et al., 2013; Tabib-Salazar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bae et al., 2013 and Tabib-Salazar et al., 2018.

claim: Two proteins gp39 and gp76 of bacteriophage P23-45 were shown to inhibit T. thermophilus transcription.
source: Two proteins gp39 and gp76 of bacteriophage P23-45 were shown to inhibit T. thermophilus transcription (Tagami et al., 2014; Ooi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tagami et al., 2014 and Ooi et al., 2018.

claim: RNAP is a validated antibacterial target.
source: Importantly, RNAP is a validated antibacterial target and novel inhibitors of RNAP hold promise for potential new antibiotic development against antimicrobial resistance (Ho et al., 2009; Srivastava et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2009; Srivastava et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2016.

claim: Purified Ocr co-eluted with RNAP in gel filtration experiments.
source: We observed that purified Ocr co-eluted with RNAP in gel filtration experiments, suggesting a tight interaction of RNAP and Ocr sufficient to withstand the lengthy elution time of the complex during chromatography (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: The binding affinity (dissociation constant, Kd) of Ocr with RNAP is in the order of 10 nM.
source: Our results show the binding affinity (dissociation constant, Kd) is in the order of 10 nM, similar to that of RNAP with sigma factors (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by MST experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The binding affinity of Ocr with RNAP is similar to that of RNAP with sigma factors.
source: Our results show the binding affinity (dissociation constant, Kd) is in the order of 10 nM, similar to that of RNAP with sigma factors (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by MST experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The affinity of Ocr for RNAP is about three orders of magnitude lower than the values reported for the association of Ocr with the EcoKI type I restriction modification enzyme.
source: Our observed affinity of Ocr for RNAP is about three orders of magnitude lower than the values reported for the association of Ocr with the EcoKI type I restriction modification enzyme (Atanasiu et al., 2002) as would be expected if the type I RM enzyme was the primary target for Ocr.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited data from Atanasiu et al., 2002.

claim: Two distinct structural classes of RNAP-Ocr complexes were identified due to their widely differing RNAP clamp conformations.
source: During 3D classification, it is clear that a number of different conformational and structural classes exist within the dataset and two distinct classes were identified due to their widely differing RNAP clamp conformations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryoEM data processing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The RNAP clamp is highly dynamic and adapts a range of conformations from closed to open involving more than 20 Å movement and 20° rotation of the clamp.
source: The RNAP clamp is highly dynamic and single-molecule Forster Resonant Energy Transfer data have shown that the RNAP clamp adapts a range of conformations from closed to open involving more than 20 Å movement and 20o rotation of the clamp (Chakraborty et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chakraborty et al., 2012.

claim: Ocr remains as a dimer upon binding to RNAP.
source: In both of the distinct RNAP-Ocr complex structures, Ocr remains as a dimer upon binding to RNAP (Figure 2A–B) and the Ocr dimers are slightly less bent compared to that of an Ocr alone crystal structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figures 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The Ocr dimers are slightly less bent compared to that of an Ocr alone crystal structure.
source: In both of the distinct RNAP-Ocr complex structures, Ocr remains as a dimer upon binding to RNAP (Figure 2A–B) and the Ocr dimers are slightly less bent compared to that of an Ocr alone crystal structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the wide clamp structure, the entire Ocr dimer inserts deeply into the RNAP cleft, occupying the full RNAP nucleic acid binding channel.
source: In one structure, the entire Ocr dimer inserts deeply into the RNAP cleft, occupying the full RNAP nucleic acid binding channel including where the transcription bubble and the downstream DNA resides in the transcriptional open and transcribing complex (Figure 2A, Figure 2C, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figures 2A, 2C, and 3A.

claim: In the wide clamp structure, the RNAP clamp is wide open and both Ocr subunits are involved in the interactions.
source: In this interaction mode, the RNAP clamp is wide open and both Ocr subunits are involved in the interactions (Figure 2A, Figure 3B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3), we thus denote it as the 'wide clamp structure'.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figures 2A, 3B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the narrow clamp structure, only one of the two Ocr subunits within the dimer contacts RNAP, occupying only the downstream DNA channel.
source: The second structure involves only one of the two Ocr subunits within the dimer contacting RNAP, occupying only the downstream DNA channel.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the narrow clamp structure, the RNAP clamp is less open.
source: Here the RNAP clamp is less open and we denote this structure the 'narrow clamp structure' (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The proximal Ocr subunit is deeply embedded in the RNAP cleft and occupies the space for the template strand DNA, the complementary newly synthesised RNA and the non-template strand DNA.
source: The proximal subunit is deeply embedded in the RNAP cleft and occupies the space for the template strand DNA, the complementary newly synthesised RNA and the non-template strand DNA (Figure 2 and Figure 3, magenta [Bae et al., 2015; Zuo and Steitz, 2015; Glyde et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figures 2 and 3, and comparison with cited structures.

claim: The distal Ocr subunit occupies the position of the downstream DNA.
source: The distal Ocr subunit occupies the position of the downstream DNA (Figure 2 and Figure 3A, yellow).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figures 2 and 3A.

claim: The negatively charged surface of the proximal Ocr complements the highly positively charged surface of the surrounding RNAP and fits snugly into the channel formed by β and β' subunits.
source: The negatively charged surface of the proximal Ocr complements the highly positively charged surface of the surrounding RNAP and fits snugly into the channel formed by β and β' subunits (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing charge complementarity in Figures 3C-E.

claim: The β' clamp has to open up to ~58 Å in RNAP-Ocr from ~35 Å in RPo to accommodate the Ocr dimer.
source: Consequently, in order to maintain the interactions between both Ocr subunits and RNAP, the β' clamp has to open up (to ~58 Å in RNAP-Ocr from ~35 Å in RPo) to accommodate the Ocr dimer compared to RPo that accommodates a transcriptional bubble and dsDNA (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the narrow clamp mode, the clamp is more open (~45 Å) compared to that in RPo (~35 Å).
source: In the narrow clamp mode, the proximal Ocr subunit interacts with the β' clamp, again mimicking downstream DNA in RPo although the clamp is more open (~45 Å) compared to that in RPo (~35 Å) (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by structural measurements shown in Figures 2B-C.

claim: Adding 5 μM Ocr decreased activity of RNAP-σ70 on different promoters in the range of 70–10%.
source: Our data reveal that adding 5 μM Ocr decreased activity of RNAP-σ70 on the different promoters in the range of 70–10%.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro transcription assay data shown in Figures 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: On the linear promoter in the presence of 5 μM Ocr the amount of spRNA was significantly reduced (to 10–30%) when Ocr was added prior to or after the holoenzyme formation but before DNA was added.
source: On the linear promoter in the presence of 5 μM Ocr the amount of spRNA was significantly reduced (to 10–30%) when Ocr was added prior to or after the holoenzyme formation but before DNA was added (Figure 5A-B I-II).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro transcription assay data shown in Figures 5A-B.

claim: The effect of Ocr after DNA was added was less pronounced.
source: However, the effect of Ocr after DNA was added was less pronounced (Figure 5A–B III).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro transcription assay data shown in Figures 5A-B.

claim: Over-expression of Ocr in E. coli cells inhibits cell growth.
source: using a reporter assay, we show that over-express of Ocr in E. coli cells inhibits cell growth (C) and β-galactosidase activities (D).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Over-expression of Ocr in E. coli cells inhibits β-galactosidase activities.
source: using a reporter assay, we show that over-express of Ocr in E. coli cells inhibits cell growth (C) and β-galactosidase activities (D).
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: An Ocr-mediated growth inhibition effect was observed in minimal modified M9 media.
source: An Ocr-mediated growth inhibition effect was indeed observed in minimal modified M9 media (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: During the 5 hr period following induction with IPTG, a ~ 10 fold decrease of normalised β-galactosidase activity was observed in E. coli cells expressing Ocr compared to cells that do not express Ocr.
source: During the 5 hr period following induction with IPTG, a ~ 10 fold decrease of normalised β-galactosidase activity was observed in E. coli cells expressing Ocr compared to cells that do not express Ocr (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by β-galactosidase activity data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Ocr was observed to inhibit RNAP-σ70 holoenzyme formation in a concentration dependent fashion.
source: Using purified components and gel mobility shift assays, Ocr was observed to inhibit RNAP-σ70 holoenzyme formation in a concentration dependent fashion and irrespective of whether Ocr is added before or after σ (Figure 6A and B, comparing lane 6 with 7–10).
evidence: This is supported by gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figures 6A and B.

claim: Appearance of a RNAP-Ocr complex accompanies the disappearance of the RNAP-σ70 holoenzyme.
source: Direct competition experiments with pre-formed RNAP-σ70 holoenzyme show that appearance of a RNAP-Ocr complex accompanies the disappearance of the RNAP-σ70 holoenzyme, (Figure 6A and B, comparing lane 6 with lanes 11–12).
evidence: This is supported by gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figures 6A and B.

claim: Ocr can displace σ70 with an apparent Kd of ~20 nM.
source: Indeed, MST experiment of Ocr binding to RNAP-σ70 revealed that Ocr can displace σ70 with an apparent Kd of ~20 nM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by MST data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ocr clearly inhibits the formation of a RNAP-σ70-DNA complex in a concentration dependent manner.
source: Ocr clearly inhibits the formation of a RNAP-σ70-DNA complex in a concentration dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: Adding 5 μM Ocr either before or after σ addition resulted in ~30% promoter complex formation.
source: Adding 5 μM Ocr either before or after σ addition resulted in ~30% promoter complex formation (Figure 6C–D,I–II).
evidence: This is supported by gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: Adding Ocr after DNA has only limited effects.
source: Adding Ocr after DNA has only limited effects (Figure 6C–D III).
evidence: This is supported by gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: Ocr inhibits RNAP recruitment to the promoter DNA by directly competing with σ for RNAP binding.
source: Together our binding experiments and in vitro transcription assays support the proposal that Ocr inhibits RNAP recruitment to the promoter DNA by directly competing with σ for RNAP binding.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental data including gel mobility shift assays, MST, and in vitro transcription assays (Figures 5, 6).

claim: Ocr has only limited effects on pre-formed RNAP-σ-DNA complexes.
source: However, Ocr has only limited effects on pre-formed RNAP-σ-DNA complexes.
evidence: This is supported by gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: Ocr is a bifunctional DNA mimic protein.
source: Our data here characterise a new activity for Ocr in inhibiting the host transcriptional machinery in addition to its established role in inhibiting the type I RM systems of the host. Thus, Ocr is a bifunctional DNA mimic protein.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing Ocr inhibits both RM systems and transcription.

claim: The structures of Ocr-RNAP show that Ocr occupies the space where σ binds.
source: The structures of Ocr-RNAP show that Ocr occupies the space where σ binds (Figure 7A–B) and where the transcription bubble and downstream DNA reside in the open complex and elongation complex, thus explaining how Ocr inhibits RNAP recruitment by σ (Vassylyev et al., 2007; Zuo and Steitz, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figures 7A-B and comparison with cited structures.

claim: Ocr occupies the space where the transcription bubble and downstream DNA reside in the open complex and elongation complex.
source: The structures of Ocr-RNAP show that Ocr occupies the space where σ binds (Figure 7A–B) and where the transcription bubble and downstream DNA reside in the open complex and elongation complex, thus explaining how Ocr inhibits RNAP recruitment by σ (Vassylyev et al., 2007; Zuo and Steitz, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figures 7A-B and comparison with cited structures.

claim: Expression of gp0.3 (Ocr) resulted in a delayed inhibition of host β-galactosidase synthesis and delayed inhibition of total RNA synthesis.
source: An earlier study by McAllister and Barrett used host strains lacking the host restriction systems, thus eliminating the effects of Ocr on host restriction enzymes. They showed that expression of gp0.3 (Ocr) resulted in a delayed inhibition of host β-galactosidase synthesis and delayed inhibition of total RNA synthesis (McAllister and Barrett, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McAllister and Barrett, 1977.

claim: Gp2 specifically inhibits σ70-dependent transcription through the interactions and stabilisation of the position of the inhibitory region 1.1 of σ70, between the β and β' clamps at the rim of the downstream DNA binding channel.
source: Structural and biochemical studies show that gp2 specifically inhibits σ70-dependent transcription through the interactions and stabilisation of the position of the inhibitory region 1.1 of σ70, between the β and β' clamps at the rim of the downstream DNA binding channel (Figure 7B; Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bae et al., 2013 and structural comparison shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Gp39 binds at region 4 of σA and restricts its conformation so that it is unable to bind to −35 promoter regions.
source: Gp39 binds at region 4 of σA and restricts its conformation so that it is unable to bind to −35 promoter regions (Figure 7C; Tagami et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tagami et al., 2014 and structural comparison shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Gp76 binds deeply in the RNAP cleft, preventing open complex formation as well as transcription elongation.
source: Gp76 on the other hand, binds deeply in the RNAP cleft, preventing open complex formation as well as transcription elongation (Figure 7D; Ooi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ooi et al., 2018 and structural comparison shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The binding site of gp76 is adjacent to, but not overlapping the σ70 region σ3.2, thus gp76 does not inhibit holoenzyme formation.
source: However, the binding site of gp76 is adjacent to, but not overlapping the σ70 region σ3.2, thus gp76 does not inhibit holoenzyme formation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Ocr inhibits holoenzyme formation per se and can disrupt a pre-formed holoenzyme.
source: Ocr on the other hand, inhibits holoenzyme formation per se and can disrupt a pre-formed holoenzyme (Figure 6A–B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figures 6A-B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ocr can also inhibit open complex formation but is unable to effectively disrupt pre-formed open complex.
source: In addition, Ocr can also inhibit open complex formation but is unable to effectively disrupt pre-formed open complex (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by gel mobility shift assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ocr was shown to mimic a dsDNA in both shape and charge distribution.
source: Ocr was shown to mimic a dsDNA in both shape and charge distribution (Walkinshaw et al., 2002) and an Ocr dimer mimics a slightly bent B-form DNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walkinshaw et al., 2002.

claim: Ocr has been shown to occupy the DNA binding grooves of type I RM enzymes through specific interactions.
source: Ocr has been shown to occupy the DNA binding grooves of type I RM enzymes through specific interactions, thus preventing viral DNA from being degraded or modified by the host RM system (Atanasiu et al., 2002; Kennaway et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Atanasiu et al., 2002 and Kennaway et al., 2009.

claim: Ocr binds in the cleft, surrounded on three sides by RNAP.
source: Ocr, on the other hand, binds in the cleft, surrounded on three sides by RNAP.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Both Ocr-RNAP and Ocr-M.EcoKI complexes are sufficiently stable to persist during lengthy size exclusion chromatography experiments.
source: Therefore it is not surprising that both Ocr-RNAP and Ocr-M.EcoKI complexes are sufficiently stable to persist during lengthy size exclusion chromatography experiments (Figure 1 and Atanasiu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 1 and citation to Atanasiu et al., 2002.

claim: Ocr remains as a dimer and binds at the downstream DNA channel of RNAP via the complementary charge interactions between the positively charged RNAP channel and the negatively charged Ocr dimer.
source: In this work, we show that Ocr remains as a dimer and binds at the downstream DNA channel of RNAP via the complementary charge interactions between the positively charged RNAP channel and the negatively charged Ocr dimer.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Due to the extensive positively charged surface within RNAP, the binding is not specific.
source: However, due to the extensive positively charged surface within RNAP, the binding is not specific.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing charge complementarity and multiple binding modes (Figures 2, 3).

claim: Two distinct binding modes have been detected which allow either the proximal or distal Ocr monomer to interact with the positively charged β' clamp.
source: Indeed, two distinct binding modes have been detected which allow either the proximal or distal Ocr monomer to interact with the positively charged β' clamp.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing two distinct RNAP-Ocr structures (Figures 2A-B).

claim: The structural flexibility of RNAP clamp plays a key role in its ability to accommodate Ocr.
source: These structures demonstrate that the structural flexibility of RNAP clamp plays a key role in its ability to accommodate Ocr.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing different clamp conformations in the two RNAP-Ocr structures (Figures 2, 3, 4).

claim: The rigidity and the bent conformation of the Ocr dimer imposes constraints on the binding sites, which are optimised for the RM enzymes it inhibits but can still be accommodated by the structurally flexible RNAP DNA binding channel.
source: However, the rigidity and the bent conformation of the Ocr dimer imposes constraints on the binding sites, which are optimised for the RM enzymes it inhibits but can still be accommodated by the structurally flexible RNAP DNA binding channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and comparison with Ocr-RM enzyme structures.

claim: Ocr could be modified to fine-tune its DNA mimicry for binding to specific DNA processing proteins.
source: Work presented here suggests that Ocr could be modified to fine-tune its DNA mimicry for binding to specific DNA processing proteins, either by reducing the rigidity of the dimer or changing the bend angle to create a new dimer interface.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the structural insights gained from this work.

claim: DNA mimicry has been proposed as a potential effective therapeutic tool.
source: DNA mimicry has been proposed as a potential effective therapeutic tool (Putnam and Tainer, 2005; Dryden, 2006; Roberts et al., 2012), Ocr could thus be exploited to create specific variants that can target specific DNA binding proteins, especially those that are shown to be antibiotic targets.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Putnam and Tainer, 2005; Dryden, 2006; Roberts et al., 2012.

claim: Ocr can effectively inhibit transcription under stress conditions when transcriptional activity is reduced.
source: In addition, our data here show that Ocr can effectively inhibit transcription under stress conditions when transcriptional activity is reduced.
evidence: This is supported by the growth inhibition data in minimal M9 media (Figure 5C).

claim: The wide clamp structure was refined to a global resolution of 3.7 Å.
source: Two classes with clear density for Ocr were refined to a global resolution 3.7 and 3.8 Å respectively although the quality is not uniform in the reconstruction, as demonstrated in the resolution distribution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the cryoEM structures.

claim: The narrow clamp structure was refined to a global resolution of 3.8 Å.
source: Two classes with clear density for Ocr were refined to a global resolution 3.7 and 3.8 Å respectively although the quality is not uniform in the reconstruction, as demonstrated in the resolution distribution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the cryoEM structures.

claim: The binding affinity between RNAP-σ and DNA is 0.1 nM for σ70 and 3 nM for σ54.
source: This is consistent with the higher binding affinity between RNAP-σ and DNA (0.1 nM for σ70 and 3 nM σ54) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) compared to RNAP-Ocr (Figure 1D).
